source.title: Fitting Very Flexible Models: Linear Regression With Large Numbers of Parameters

record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out prediction error across model sizes in a linear-regression toy experiment, testing double descent with a different model class and setup from the deep-network claim.
record.gate_note: Figure 9 reports cross-validation mean squared error for feature-weighted OLS across p and compares it with ridge regression. The text describes the qualitative outcomes, but the plotted values are not given numerically, so values are recorded as figure only. The Gaussian-process line has no associated p and is not a model-size sweep. Results cited from other studies, including early stopping, are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Figure 9 is the note's own sweep of held-out (leave-one-out) error against parameter count p for Fourier-basis linear regression (n = 23). It shows a peak near p ≈ n and recovery at large p, with and without ridge. This is a new model class and setting with its own result on the general double-descent curve. The note says it brings no new theory, but the sweep is its own.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also argue that over-fitting comes from p being comparable to n combined with inappropriate regularization, not from large p. They attribute the peak to estimator variance from ill-conditioned matrices, which amplify noise. They recommend large p with deliberate regularization, chosen by cross-validation.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses Fourier-basis linear regression and leave-one-out cross-validation on toy data, rather than deep-network experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported behavior differs between feature-weighted OLS and ridge regression with λ = 0.1.
record.peer_reviewed: Publications of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific
record.problems: The result is illustrated on toy data with n = 23. Figure 9 gives no numeric CVMSE values or uncertainty estimates. The study does not test deep networks, epoch-wise descent, sample-size changes, label-noise effects, or optimal regularization tuning.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying results left out. The Gaussian-process curve in Figure 9 is flat because it has no associated p; the other figures show fits or uncertainty illustrations rather than test-error sweeps.

untested.parts: Model classes other than Fourier-basis linear regression; data other than one toy set.
Whether label noise or variance drives the peak (given only as an ill-conditioning argument, not measured); multiple peaks; optimal tuning of regularization.

missing.what: The Gaussian-process CVMSE (the p → ∞ limit of feature-weighted OLS) as the infinite-capacity endpoint. It is shown as a flat line comparable to large-p OLS, and the text says the fits are essentially identical.

record.verdict_notes: This is a tutorial note on a single toy dataset (n = 23), with no numeric values or uncertainties. The early-stopping and dimensionality-reduction removal of the peak are cited results (Hastie et al.; Huang et al.) and are correctly left out as rows. The record's V4 limits_scope label based on r2 is removed: the ridge result bears on V6's regularization claim, not on V4.

versions.untested_parts: Changing training sample size near the interpolation threshold.
Other model classes beyond the illustrated linear-regression setting.
A single effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample size.
Whether label noise or variance drives the peak; multiple or triple descent; and whether the regularization is optimally tuned.
Whether measuring complexity by an effective parameter count turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: feature-weighted OLS
rows.operation_detail: Sweep the number of Fourier-basis features p and measure leave-one-out cross-validation mean squared prediction error.

conditions.value: weight function from equations (21) and (22), s = 0.05
first and last data points omitted from the mean squared error

rows.measure: Leave-one-out cross-validation mean squared prediction error (CVMSE)
rows.note: The text says CVMSE is much worse at p approximately n than at very low or very high p. The figure plots the sweep, but does not provide numeric CVMSE values.
rows.check: Should link to V4 only. This row varies neither noise nor regularization, so it does not bear on V6. The text says CVMSE is 'much, much worse at p ≈ n' than at very low or very high p. Values are figure only. At high p the curve saturates because feature weights underflow. The first and last points are excluded from the MSE.

rows.subject: ridge regression
rows.operation_detail: Sweep p and measure leave-one-out cross-validation mean squared prediction error with ridge regularization.

conditions.value: first and last data points omitted from the mean squared error

rows.measure: Leave-one-out cross-validation mean squared prediction error (CVMSE)
rows.note: The text says ridge regression does not show the high-risk behavior near p approximately n. The plotted values are not stated numerically. The paper says λ = 0.1 was chosen heuristically by hand; it does not report optimal tuning.
rows.check: Should link to V6 (regularization removes the peak), not V4. A ridge curve without a peak does not bear on whether risk recovers past interpolation. λ = 0.1 was hand-chosen, not optimally tuned. The comparison may also be confounded: ridge appears to use unweighted features, while the OLS curve uses feature weighting, so two things change at once.

relationships.condition: Feature-weighted min-norm OLS, Fourier basis, toy data, n = 23
relationships.reason: Leave-one-out CVMSE peaks by orders of magnitude at p ≈ n and falls again at p ≫ n (r1, figure only).
relationships.display_finding: Leave-one-out cross-validation MSE peaked by orders of magnitude near p=n and fell again when p≫n.

relationships.condition: Ridge regression with hand-chosen λ = 0.1 on the same toy data
relationships.reason: Text and Figure 9: ridge regression does not show the p ≈ n peak, so regularization removes it even without optimal tuning (r2, figure only).
relationships.display_finding: Ridge with λ = 0.1 showed no peak near p = n.
